analysis.one_liner: Gives tax credits so uninsured people can buy private health insurance, expands Medicare benefits, and limits malpractice lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 1990 with three Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it; it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill offered a refundable tax credit covering part of the cost of private health insurance for people who don't get coverage through an employer, with the money advanced during the year as certificates usable to buy a policy. It added Medicare benefits — screening mammograms, in-home respite care, longer hospice coverage, broader home health — paid for partly by higher monthly Medicare premiums. It also rewrote medical malpractice rules nationwide so the losing side pays legal fees and each defendant pays only their own share of fault, and it created a government seal of approval for insurance policies sold to seniors.
analysis.who_benefits: People without employer coverage — especially lower-income households, who could get the credit advanced during the year as certificates to buy a private policy. Medicare beneficiaries would gain new covered services. Rural hospitals and residents would benefit from payment equalization, doctor recruitment priorities, and grants to county health departments. Buyers of long-term care insurance and seniors shopping for supplemental (Medigap) policies would get tax credits and a certification program. Health insurers gain a new subsidized customer base.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured people, seniors, and rural communities

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for 60% of health insurance premiums (counted up to $1,200 for singles, $2,400 for joint filers) for people not covered by an employer plan, phasing out at higher incomes.
Lets people below 1.49 times the poverty line receive the credit in advance, as certificates usable to buy insurance during the year rather than waiting for tax filing.

Adds Medicare coverage of screening mammography with quality standards and limits on what doctors can charge, plus up to 80 hours a year of in-home respite care for chronically dependent beneficiaries, an extra hospice period, and broader home health coverage.

Creates a tax credit for long-term care insurance premiums, exempts early retirement withdrawals used for such premiums from the 10% penalty tax, and treats long-term care plans like health plans for tax purposes.

Directs elimination of separate Medicare payment rates for rural versus urban hospitals, prioritizes National Health Service Corps placements in underserved areas, funds grants to county health departments for preventive services, and reauthorizes immunization grants with a six-month federal vaccine stockpile.

Establishes a Health and Human Services certification — printed as an emblem on qualifying policies — for senior health insurance policies meeting minimum standards on renewability, preexisting-condition limits, and plain language, to protect seniors from confusing or unsafe Medigap sales.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries would pay higher Part B monthly premiums (80 cents to $1.30 more per month from 1991 through 1995) to finance the new benefits. Injured patients would bear the malpractice changes: losing plaintiffs would owe the other side's legal fees, and defendants would no longer be jointly liable for a plaintiff's full damages when others cannot pay. Taxpayers fund the rural, immunization, and grant programs, and the refundable credits are a federal cost.

drawbacks.text: The malpractice title applies loser-pays to all medical malpractice cases in state and federal court and abolishes joint and several liability, so an injured patient who loses — or whose portion of fault another liable party cannot pay — absorbs costs that today's rules place on defendants. Patients with valid claims but limited means could be deterred from suing at all.

The insurance credit is capped: at most $720 for a single filer and $1,440 for a joint return, and only for people without employer coverage — likely too small, on its own, to make a private policy affordable for many low-income families, and it offers no guarantee that insurers would sell to them at any price.
The new Medicare benefits are financed by increasing the Part B premium that every enrollee pays, so the seniors receiving the new coverage also pay for it, regardless of whether they use it.

The long-term care title creates tax-preferred private long-term care insurance, but eligibility for the advance payment is limited to people under 1.49 times the poverty line and the credit phases out above $25,000–$40,000 of income, limiting its reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes real help with real costs. The insurance credit would put modest money in the hands of people buying coverage on their own, and the Medicare additions — mammography screening, respite care, hospice and home health expansion, plus the Medigap certification seal — are concrete benefits. But the design has serious weaknesses: the credit is small relative to what individual coverage costs and comes with no requirement that insurers offer affordable policies, so it may subsidize purchases without guaranteeing coverage. The malpractice title shifts financial risk from doctors and their insurers onto injured patients through loser-pays fees and the end of joint liability. And the Medicare improvements are paid for by premiums on beneficiaries themselves. The malpractice title in particular is a significant concession to providers at patients' expense, which an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: McConnell introduced the bill in late April 1990 and it went straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or vote on it; it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Mitch McConnell introduced the Comprehensive American Health Care Act on April 27, 1990, with three Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly. The existing system stayed intact: doctors, their malpractice insurers, and health insurers were spared the bill's malpractice restrictions and new regulatory certification, while the uninsured and Medicare beneficiaries never received its new benefits and credits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; insurers and providers kept the status quo

for.name: Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its comprehensive health plan in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Lloyd Bentsen, D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no action — no markup, no vote — for the remaining eight months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only four senators — all Republicans — are on record in support, and no one is recorded in opposition; the bill never progressed far enough for a partisan split to show.

industries.note: The bill routes its help for the uninsured entirely through private insurance: refundable tax credits and advance certificates can only be used to buy private coverage, making insurers the permanent channel for the subsidy. It also gives qualifying senior policies a federal certification seal, which legitimizes the Medigap market even while setting minimum standards for it.

The malpractice title imposes loser-pays legal fees and ends joint and several liability in every malpractice case nationwide, cutting providers' and their insurers' exposure. The cost of that shift falls on injured patients, whose recovery can come up short when other at-fault parties cannot pay.

Loser-pays fee-shifting and mandatory disclosure of settlement alternatives reduce malpractice litigation and its contingency-fee economics. Their interest tracks injured patients', who lose legal recourse under the same provisions.

The bill directs a methodology to eliminate separate Medicare payment rates for rural hospitals with a floor guaranteeing no hospital receives less than it did in October 1990, and orders a review of easing rural hospital staffing regulations.

industries.industry: Long-term care insurance and vaccine makers
industries.note: Tax preferences and a premium credit steer purchasers toward private long-term care insurance, and the reauthorized immunization program plus a CDC six-month vaccine stockpile create guaranteed public purchases of vaccines.
